meta.title: Assessing the impact of off-nadir image acquisition on the performance of a deep learning model for on-board ship segmentation
meta.authorsHtml: Francesco Pasanisi<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Tom Hendrix<sup>1</sup>, David Rijlaarsdam<sup>1</sup>, Aubrey Dunne<sup>2</sup>
affiliations: 1Ubotica Technologies, Kluyverweg 1 2629HS Delft, the Netherlands 2Ubotica Technologies, D11 KXN4 Dublin, Ireland

abstract: Off-nadir image acquisition substantially increases the revisit frequency of agile imaging satellites such as CogniSAT- 6, yet its impact on deep learning model performance for ship segmentation remains unstudied. This paper presents an evaluation of off-nadir acquisition (ONA) effects on a CNN-based ship segmentation model, using 38 annotated CogniSAT-6 scenes spanning the full 0°–45° roll angle range, organized into four viewing angle bins. Contrary to findings from building detection studies, no statistically significant relationship was found between viewing angle and model performance (R²=0.030, p=0.302). Spearman correlation analysis revealed that roll angle, sun zenith angle, and median ship size are not significant predictors of performance. Instead, the ship-water contrast ratio emerged as the only significant predictor (r=0.563, p<0.001), indicating that scene-specific spectral characteristics are a stronger determinant of segmentation quality than acquisition geometry. These findings suggest that CogniSAT-6 can operate across its full roll angle range without significant degradation in ship segmentation performance, with scene spectral characteristics being the primary factor to take into account.

blocks.html: Satellite-based maritime monitoring is a key application of Earth Observation (EO), enabling ship tracking, maritime situational awareness and environmental protection. Deep learning models for ship segmentation have shown strong performance when operating on nadir imagery; however, modern high-resolution satellites such as CogniSAT-6 [1] are capable of acquiring images at significant off-nadir angles (i.e., deviating from the vertical, straight-down direction), rolling up to 45° in the across-track direction. This offnadir acquisition (ONA) capability substantially increases temporal resolution: for CogniSAT-6, extending acquisitions from 0–15° to the full 0–45° range can reduce revisit time over major ports from approximately 7 days to under 3 days (Figure 1).

blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: However, off-nadir imaging introduces several well-known degradation mechanisms which may hinder the performance of deep learning models, especially if off-nadir imagery was not part of their training dataset. The Ground Sampling Distance (GSD) increases with viewing angle (or roll angle), reducing spatial resolution and making smaller ships harder to resolve [2]. The longer atmospheric path length amplifies Rayleigh scattering, particularly at shorter wavelengths [3, 4]. Additionally, radiometric changes due to the Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) can alter the apparent reflectance of surfaces, including ship hulls [5]. These effects are compounded by the fact that CogniSAT-6 performs no atmospheric correction or image preprocessing onboard, i.e., the ship segmentation model processes raw L0 data directly. Onboard atmospheric correction and BRDF correction are computationally prohibitive for resource-constrained small satellites like CogniSAT-6 [1, 6]. Furthermore, off-nadir imagery is largely absent from open-access datasets (such as Sentinel), as most public satellite missions acquire nadir or near-nadir imagery, with only a limited number of commercial constellations capable of significant off-nadir acquisition. This limits the availability of training data representative of offnadir conditions, both before and after launch. A visual example of the impact of ONA is shown in Figure 2. The impact of ONA on deep learning model performance has been studied primarily in the context of building detection. Results from the SpaceNet Multi-View Overhead Imagery (MVOI) dataset show a clear degradation in segmentation performance beyond viewing angles of 10–15°, with models trained on nadir imagery being particularly sensitive [7, 8]. Approaches such as nadir-like image generation via GANs have been proposed to mitigate this effect [9]. However, ships and buildings are fundamentally different targets: ships appear on a relatively uniform water back-ground, vary greatly in size, and lack the fixed geometry of buildings. No published study addresses the impact of ONA specifically on ship segmentation models, leaving a critical gap for the operational deployment of agile imaging satellites. This paper presents a systematic evaluation of ONA effects on a ship segmentation model, using CogniSAT-6 imagery spanning the full 0°–45° roll angle range, revealing that viewing angle has a surprisingly limited impact on model performance compared to scene-specific factors such as ship-water contrast ratio. To isolate the effect of viewing angle from other potentially confounding scene-level factors, illumination conditions and ship size are also examined alongside acquisition geometry.

blocks.html: The dataset used in this study consists of 38 annotated CogniSAT-6 scenes acquired over major seaports worldwide. Scenes are organised into four viewing angle bins based on the satellite’s roll angle, as shown in Table 1. The bin boundaries were chosen based on the GSD increase with viewing angle for the optical sensor onboard CogniSAT-6 (Figure 3) and findings from the building detection literature suggesting performance degradation beyond 10–15°. For each scene, three ground truth masks were available: a ship mask, a land mask, and a cloud mask. Scenes were tiled into 256×256 pixel patches, with tiles containing land or cloud coverage above 0% discarded, retaining only open-water tiles. Ships with an area smaller than 20 pixels were excluded from the analysis to minimize the influence of small ship size on the evaluation results, ensuring that observed performance differences are more attributable to viewing angle effects.

blocks.html: The ship segmentation model evaluated in this study, which was developed by Ubotica Technologies, is a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for semantic segmentation of ships, and is based on a UNet architecture [10]. The model takes 256×256 pixel RGB tiles as input and outputs a binary ship mask. The images in the dataset for this study were not used for training, and the used model was trained only on nadir or near-nadir imagery, making this evaluation a zero-shot assessment of its generalization to off-nadir conditions. In this study, model performance is evaluated using Dice Score:

where P is the predicted binary mask and G is the ground truth mask. The evaluation is performed at tile level and aggregated to scene level, as tiles within the same scene share identical acquisition conditions and are not independent observations. The Dice Score is preferred as it is less sensitive to boundary precision, which is less critical in ship detection than correctly identifying the presence of a vessel. Four analyses were conducted. First, Dice Score distributions are compared across the four viewing angle bins using boxplots, with scene-level weighted averages to account for uneven ship distribution. Second, a simple linear regression is performed between roll angle and Dice Score to quantify and assess the statistical significance of any viewing angle effect. Third, a Spearman correlation analysis examines the relationship between Dice Score and multiple scene-level factors: roll angle, sun zenith angle, and median ship size. where di is the difference between the ranks of corresponding observations and n is the number of scenes. Spearman correlation was preferred over Pearson as it makes no assumption of linearity or normality, and is more robust to the outliers present in the relatively small dataset [11]. Finally, a ship-water contrast ratio is computed for each scene, and its correlation with Dice Score is assessed in order to investigate whether spectral scene characteristics influence model performance independently of viewing geometry. The Contrast Ratio (CR) is defined as the ratio of mean ship Digital Number (DN) to mean surrounding water DN in the red band (as ship labels were annotated on top of the red band, due to band misalignment in raw L0 optical data):
where µship and µwater are the mean DN values of ship pixels and surrounding water pixels respectively in the red band.

Figure 4 shows the distribution of Dice Score, normalized to the median performance of the Nadir bin, across the four viewing angle bins. No consistent degradation is observed with increasing viewing angle, and the weighted scene averages remain relatively stable across all bins, with a slightly positive trend contrary to the degradation commonly reported in building detection studies. The substantial overlap between distributions across all bins, combined with considerable scene-to-scene variability within each bin, suggests that viewing angle is not the primary factor driving performance differences. It is worth noting that all evaluations are performed on raw L0 imagery with no atmospheric correction, representing a more challenging condition than typically reported in the ship segmentation literature.

blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: To quantify the statistical relationship between viewing angle and model performance, a simple linear regression was performed between roll angle and normalized Dice Score at scene level. Figure 5 shows the results, yielding R²=0.030 and p=0.302, indicating that viewing angle accounts for only 3% of the variance in model performance and that this relationship is not statistically significant. The slight positive slope of the regression line is consistent with the bin-level analysis, further supporting the conclusion that off-nadir acquisition does not systematically degrade ship segmentation performance.

blocks.caption: Linear regression between normalized Dice Score and roll angle.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: To investigate which scene-level factors influence model performance, a Spearman rank correlation analysis was conducted between normalised Dice Score and three variables: roll angle, sun zenith angle, and median ship size. Results are shown in Table 2. None of roll angle (r=0.152, p=0.362), sun zenith angle (r=0.096, p=0.566), or median ship size (r=-0.069, p=0.680) showed a statistically significant correlation with model performance, confirming that acquisition geometry and illumination conditions are not the primary drivers of performance variability across scenes.

blocks.html: To investigate whether spectral scene characteristics influence model performance independently of viewing geometry, a ship-water contrast ratio was computed for each scene as previously defined in Equation (3). Figure 6 shows the Spearman correlation between contrast ratio and normalized Dice Score across all 38 scenes, yielding r=0.563 and p<0.001. This is the strongest and only statistically significant predictor of model performance identified in this study, suggesting that scenes where ships are more spectrally distinct from the surrounding water are consistently easier for the model to segment, regardless of viewing angle. This finding highlights that scene-specific spectral characteristics are a more critical determinant of ship segmentation performance than acquisition geometry.

blocks.caption: Spearman correlation between Normalized Dice Score and Contrast Ratio. The red-shaded area represents the 95% confidence interval of the regression line.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: The results of this study challenge the assumption that off-nadir acquisition necessarily degrades ship segmentation performance. Unlike building detection models, which show clear performance degradation beyond 10–15° [7, 8], the evaluated model maintained relatively stable performance across the full 0°–45° roll angle range, with no statistically significant relationship between viewing angle and Dice Score (R²=0.030, p=0.302). This suggests that ship segmentation may be inherently more robust to viewing geometry changes than object detection tasks involving complex 3D structures. The only statistically significant predictor of model performance identified in this study was the ship-water contrast ratio (r=0.563, p<0.001), indicating that scene-specific spectral characteristics are a stronger determinant of segmentation quality than acquisition geometry. This finding has practical implications as satellite operators may benefit from wider roll angle ranges without worrying about model performance degradation. Complementary qualitative analysis of Planet Labs SkySat imagery [12] acquired over Dubai across different viewing angle bins revealed a progressive shift in spectral band distributions with increasing viewing angle, particularly in the blue band, consistent with increased Rayleigh scattering along longer atmospheric path lengths [3, 4] (Figure 7). Despite these measurable spectral changes, no significant performance degradation was observed in the experimental results presented, suggesting that the model is robust to such spectral variations.

The blue band shifts rightward with increasing viewing angle, consistent with Rayleigh scattering effects. blocks.html: However, this study has some limitations. The dataset is relatively small, particularly in the VOFF bin, limiting statistical power. All evaluations were performed on raw L0 imagery with no atmospheric correction, which, while representative of CogniSAT-6’s operational conditions, makes direct comparison with other studies difficult. Several potentially influential factors, such as atmospheric conditions, water turbidity, and ship type, remain unexplored and represent directions for future work. Furthermore, the GSD approximately doubling from nadir to the VOFF bin (as shown in Figure 3) means that ships of identical dimensions appear at roughly half the pixel size in very off-nadir acquisitions. While ships smaller than 20 pixels were excluded to reduce the influence of apparent ship size, and no significant performance degradation was observed in the VOFF bin, the limited number of scenes means this conclusion should be interpreted with caution. The SkySat dataset will be expanded to a quantitative spectral analysis across multiple locations and bins for cross-sensor validation.
